non-verbal <color=#3366CC>communication</color> by displaying emotions such as sadness, anger, surprise and excitement. In many other
mammals, they contain much longer, whisker-like hairs that act as tactile sensors.
The eyelash grows at the edges of the eyelid and protects the eye from dirt. The eyelash is to humans, camels, horses,
ostriches etc., what whiskers are to <color=#3366CC>cats</color>; they are used to sense when dirt, dust, or any other potentially harmful object
is too close to the eye. The eye reflexively closes as a result of this sensation.
Eyebrows and eyelashes do not grow beyond a certain length (eyelashes are rarely more than 10 mm long). However,
trichomegaly can cause the lashes to grow remarkably long and prominent (in some cases the upper lashes grow to 15
mm long).
Evolution
Hair has its origins in the common ancestor of mammals, the synapsids, about 300 million years ago. It is currently
unknown at what stage the synapsids acquired mammalian characteristics such as body hair and mammary glands, as
the fossils only rarely provide direct evidence for soft tissues. Skin impression of the belly and lower tail of a
pelycosaur, possibly Haptodus shows the basal synapsid stock bore transverse rows of rectangular scutes, similar to
those of a modern crocodile, so the age of acquirement of hair logically could not have been earlier than 299 ma, based
on the current understanding of the animal's phylogeny. An exceptionally well-preserved skull of Estemmenosuchus, a
therapsid from the Upper Permian, shows smooth, hairless skin with what appears to be glandular depressions, though
as a semi-aquatic species it might not have been particularly useful to determine the integument of terrestrial species.
The oldest undisputed known fossils showing unambiguous imprints of hair are the Callovian (late middle Jurassic)
Castorocauda and several contemporary haramiyidans, both near-mammal cynodonts, giving the age as no later than
220 ma based on the modern phylogenetic understanding of these clades. More recently, studies on terminal Permian
<color=#3366CC>Russian</color> coprolites may suggest that non-mammalian synapsids from that era had fur. If this is the case, these are the
oldest hair remnants known, showcasing that fur occurred as far back as the latest Paleozoic.
Some modern mammals have a special gland in front of each orbit used to preen the fur, called the harderian gland.
Imprints of this structure are found in the skull of the small early mammals like Morganucodon, but not in their cynodont
ancestors like Thrinaxodon.
The hairs of the fur in modern animals are all connected to nerves, and so the fur also serves as a transmitter for
sensory input. Fur could have evolved from sensory hair (whiskers). The signals from this sensory apparatus is
interpreted in the neocortex, a section of the brain that expanded markedly in animals like Morganucodon and
Hadrocodium. The more advanced therapsids could have had a combination of naked skin, whiskers, and scutes. A full
pelage likely did not evolve until the therapsid-mammal transition. The more advanced, smaller therapsids could have
had a combination of hair and scutes, a combination still found in some modern mammals, such as rodents and the
opossum.
The high interspecific variability of the size, color, and microstructure of hair often enables the identification of species
based on single hair filaments.
In varying degrees most <color=#3366CC>mammals</color> have some skin areas without natural hair. On the human body, glabrous skin is
found on the ventral portion of the fingers, palms, soles of feet and lips, which are all parts of the body most closely
associated with interacting with the world around us, as are the labia minora and glans penis. There are four main
types of mechanoreceptors in the glabrous skin of humans: Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner's corpuscles, Merkel's discs,
and Ruffini corpuscles.
The naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber) has evolved skin lacking in general, pelagic hair covering, yet has retained
long, very sparsely scattered tactile hairs over its body. Glabrousness is a trait that may be associated with neoteny.
Evolutionary variation
Primates are relatively hairless compared to other mammals, and Hominini such as chimpanzees, have less dense hair
than would be expected given their body size for a primate. Evolutionary biologists suggest that the genus Homo arose
in East Africa approximately 2 million years ago. Part of this evolution was the development of endurance running and
venturing out during the hot times of the day that required efficient thermoregulation through perspiration. The loss of
heat through heat of evaporation by means of sweat glands is aided by air currents next to the skin surface, which are
facilitated by the loss of body hair.
Another factor in human evolution that also occurred in the prehistoric past was a preferential selection for neoteny,
particularly in females. The idea that adult humans exhibit certain neotenous (juvenile) features, not evinced in the
other great apes, is about a century old. Louis Bolk made a long list of such traits, and Stephen Jay Gould published a
short list in Ontogeny and Phylogeny. In addition, paedomorphic characteristics in women are often acknowledged as
desirable by men in developed countries. For instance, vellus hair is a juvenile characteristic. However, while men
develop longer, coarser, thicker, and darker terminal hair through sexual differentiation, women do not, leaving their
vellus hair visible.
Texture
Curly hair
Jablonski asserts head hair was evolutionarily advantageous for pre-humans to retain because it protected the scalp as
they walked upright in the intense African (equatorial) UV light. While some might argue that, by this logic, humans
should also express hairy shoulders because these body parts would putatively be exposed to similar conditions, the
protection of the head, the seat of the brain that enabled humanity to become one of the most successful species on
the planet (and which also is very vulnerable at birth) was arguably a more urgent issue (axillary hair in the underarms
and groin were also retained as signs of sexual maturity). Sometime during the gradual process by which Homo
erectus began a transition from furry skin to the naked skin expressed by Homo sapiens, hair texture putatively
gradually changed from straight hair (the condition of most mammals, including humanity's closest
cousins—chimpanzees) to Afro-textured hair or 'kinky' (i.e. tightly coiled). This argument assumes that curly hair better
impedes the passage of UV light into the body relative to straight hair (thus curly or coiled hair would be particularly
advantageous for light-skinned hominids living at the equator).
It is substantiated by Iyengar's findings (1998) that UV light can enter into straight human hair roots (and thus into the
body through the skin) via the hair shaft. Specifically, the results of that study suggest that this phenomenon resembles
the passage of light through fiber optic tubes (which do not function as effectively when kinked or sharply curved or
coiled). In this sense, when hominids (i.e. Homo erectus) were gradually losing their straight body hair and thereby
exposing the initially pale skin underneath their fur to the sun, straight hair would have been an adaptive liability. By
inverse logic, later, as humans traveled farther from Africa and/or the equator, straight hair may have (initially) evolved
to aid the entry of UV light into the body during the transition from dark, UV-protected skin to paler skin.
Jablonski's assertions suggest that the adjective "woolly" in reference to Afro-hair is a misnomer in connoting the high
heat insulation derivable from the true wool of sheep. Instead, the relatively sparse density of Afro-hair, combined with
its springy coils actually results in an airy, almost sponge-like structure that in turn, Jablonski argues, more likely
facilitates an increase in the circulation of cool air onto the scalp. Further, wet Afro-hair does not stick to the neck and
scalp unless totally drenched and instead tends to retain its basic springy puffiness because it less easily responds to
moisture and sweat than straight hair does. In this sense, the trait may enhance comfort levels in intense equatorial
climates more than straight hair (which, on the other hand, tends to naturally fall over the ears and neck to a degree
that provides slightly enhanced comfort levels in cold climates relative to tightly coiled hair).
Further, it is notable that the most pervasive expression of this hair texture can be found in sub-Saharan Africa; a
region of the world that abundant genetic and paleo-anthropological evidence suggests, was the relatively recent
(200,000-year-old) point of origin for modern humanity. In fact, although genetic findings (Tishkoff, 2009) suggest that
sub-Saharan Africans are the most genetically diverse continental group on Earth, Afro-textured hair approaches
ubiquity in this region. This points to a strong, long-term selective pressure that, in stark contrast to most other regions
of the genomes of sub-Saharan groups, left little room for genetic variation at the determining loci. Such a pattern,
again, does not seem to support human sexual aesthetics as being the sole or primary cause of this distribution.
The EDAR locus
A group of studies have recently shown that genetic patterns at the EDAR locus, a region of the modern human
genome that contributes to hair texture variation among most individuals of East Asian descent, support the hypothesis
that (East Asian) straight hair likely developed in this branch of the modern human lineage subsequent to the original
expression of tightly coiled natural afro-hair. Specifically, the relevant findings indicate that the EDAR mutation coding
for the predominant East Asian 'coarse' or thick, straight hair texture arose within the past 65,000 years, which is a time
frame that covers from the earliest of the 'Out of Africa' migrations up to now.
Disease
Ringworm is a fungal disease that targets hairy skin.
Premature greying of hair is another condition that results in greying before the age of 20 years in Europeans, before
25 years in Asians, and before 30 years in Africans.
Hair care
Hair care involves the <color=#3366CC>hygiene</color> and cosmetology of hair including hair on the scalp, facial hair (beard and moustache),
pubic hair and other body hair. Hair care routines differ according to an individual's culture and the physical
characteristics of one's hair. Hair may be colored, trimmed, shaved, plucked, or otherwise removed with treatments
such as waxing, sugaring, and threading.
Removal practices
Depilation is the removal of hair from the surface of the skin. This can be achieved through methods such as shaving.
Epilation is the removal of the entire hair strand, including the part of the hair that has not yet left the follicle. A popular
way to epilate hair is through waxing.
Shaving
Shaving is accomplished with bladed instruments, such as razors. The blade is brought close to the skin and stroked
over the hair in the desired area to cut the terminal hairs and leave the skin feeling smooth. Depending upon the rate of
growth, one can begin to feel the hair growing back within hours of shaving. This is especially evident in men who
develop a five o'clock shadow after having shaved their faces. This new growth is called stubble. Stubble typically
appears to grow back thicker because the shaved hairs are blunted instead of tapered off at the end, although the hair
never actually grows back thicker.
Waxing
Waxing involves using a sticky wax and strip of paper or cloth to pull hair from the root. Waxing is the ideal hair removal
technique to keep an area hair-free for long periods of time. It can take three to five weeks for waxed hair to begin to
resurface again. Hair in areas that have been waxed consistently is known to grow back finer and thinner, especially
compared to hair that has been shaved with a razor.
Laser removal
Laser hair removal is a cosmetic method where a small <color=#3366CC>laser</color> beam pulses selective heat on dark target matter in the
area that causes hair growth without harming the skin tissue. This process is repeated several times over the course of
many months to a couple of years with hair regrowing less frequently until it finally stops; this is used as a more
permanent solution to waxing or shaving. Laser removal is practiced in many clinics along with many at-home products.
Cutting and trimming
Because the hair on one's head is normally longer than other types of body hair, it is cut with scissors or clippers.
People with longer hair will most often use scissors to cut their hair, whereas shorter hair is maintained using a trimmer.
Depending on the desired length and overall health of the hair, periods without cutting or trimming the hair can vary.
Cut hair may be used in wigs. Global imports of hair in 2010 was worth $US 1.24 billion.
Social role
Hair has great social significance for human beings. It can grow on most external areas of the <color=#3366CC>human body</color>, except on
the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet (among other areas). Hair is most noticeable on most people in a small
number of areas, which are also the ones that are most commonly trimmed, plucked, or shaved. These include the
face, <color=#3366CC>ears</color>, head, eyebrows, legs, and armpits, as well as the pubic region. The highly visible differences between male
and female body and facial hair are a notable secondary sex characteristic.
The world's longest documented hair belongs to Xie Qiuping (in <color=#3366CC>China</color>), at 5.627 m when measured on 8 May 2004.
She has been growing her hair since 1973, from the age of 13.
Indication of status
Healthy hair indicates health and youth (important in evolutionary biology). Hair color and texture can be a sign of
ethnic ancestry. Facial hair is a sign of puberty in men. White or gray hair is a sign of age or genetics, which may be
concealed with hair dye (not easily for some), although many prefer to assume it (especially if it is a poliosis
characteristic of the person since childhood). Pattern baldness in men is usually seen as a sign of aging that may be
concealed with a toupee, hats, or religious and cultural adornments; however, the condition can be triggered by various
hormonal factors at any age following puberty and is not uncommon in younger men. Although pattern baldness can be
slowed down by drugs such as Finasteride and Minoxidil or treated with hair transplants, many men see this as
unnecessary effort for the sake of vanity and instead shave their heads. In early modern China, the queue was a male
hairstyle in which the hair at the front and top was shaved every 10 days in a style mimicking pattern baldness, while
the remaining hair at the back was braided into a long pigtail.
A hairstyle may be an indicator of group membership. During the English Civil War, followers of Oliver Cromwell
cropped their hair close to their head in an act of defiance against the curls and ringlets of the king's men, which led to
them being nicknamed Roundheads. Recent isotopic analysis of hair is helping to shed further light on sociocultural
interaction, giving information on food procurement and consumption in the 19th century. Having bobbed hair was
popular among the flappers in the 1920s as a sign of rebellion against traditional roles for women. Female art students
known as the Cropheads also adopted the style, notably at the Slade School in <color=#3366CC>London</color>. Regional variations in
hirsutism has caused practices regarding hair on the arms and legs to differ. Some religious groups may follow certain
rules regarding hair as part of religious observance. The rules often differ for men and women.
Many subcultures have hairstyles which may indicate an unofficial membership. Many hippies, metalheads, and Indian
sadhus have long hair, as well many older hipsters. Many punks wear a hairstyle known as a mohawk or other spiked
and dyed hairstyles, while skinheads have short-cropped or completely shaved heads. Long stylized bangs were very
common for emos, scene kids, and younger hipsters in the 2000s and early 2010s.
Heads were shaved in concentration camps, and head-shaving has been used as punishment, especially for women
with long hair. The shaven head is common in <color=#3366CC>military</color> haircuts, while Western monks are known for the tonsure. By
contrast, among some Indian holy men, the hair is worn extremely long.
In the time of Confucius (5th century BCE), the Chinese grew out their hair and often tied it, as a symbol of filial piety.
Regular hairdressing in some cultures is considered a sign of wealth or status. The dreadlocks of the Rastafari
movement were despised early in the movement's history. In some cultures, having one's hair cut can symbolize a
liberation from one's past, usually after a trying time in one's life. Cutting the hair also may be a sign of mourning.
Tightly coiled hair in its natural state may be worn in an Afro. This hairstyle was once worn among African Americans
as a symbol of racial pride. Given that the coiled texture is the natural state of some African Americans' hair, or
perceived as being more "African", this simple style is now often seen as a sign of self-acceptance and an affirmation
that the beauty norms of the (eurocentric) dominant culture are not absolute. African Americans as a whole have a
variety of hair textures, as they are not an ethnically homogeneous group, but an ad-hoc of many diverse genetic
backgrounds.
The film Easy Rider (1969) includes the assumption that the two main characters could have their long hairs forcibly
shaved with a rusty razor when jailed, symbolizing the intolerance of some conservative groups toward members of the
counterculture. At the conclusion of England's 1971 Oz trials, the defendants had their heads shaved by the police,
causing public outcry. During the appeal trial, they appeared in the dock wearing wigs. A case where a 14-year-old
student was expelled from school in Brazil in the mid-2000s, allegedly because of his fauxhawk haircut, sparked
national debate and legal action resulting in compensation.
Religious practices
Women's hair may be hidden using headscarves, a common part of the hijab in <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> and a symbol of modesty
required for certain religious rituals in <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodoxy</color>. The Russian Orthodox Church requires all married women to
wear headscarves inside the church; this tradition is often extended to all women, regardless of marital status.
Orthodox Judaism also commands the use of scarves and other head coverings for married women for modesty
reasons. Certain Hindu sects also wear head scarves for religious reasons. <color=#3366CC>Sikhs</color> have an obligation not to cut hair (a
Sikh cutting hair becomes 'apostate' which means fallen from religion) and men keep it tied in a bun on the head, which
is then covered appropriately using a turban. Multiple religions, both ancient and contemporary, require or advise one
to allow their hair to become dreadlocks, though people also wear them for fashion. For men, Islam, Orthodox Judaism,
Orthodox Christianity, Roman Catholicism, and other religious groups have at various times recommended or required
the covering of the head and sections of the hair of men, and some have dictates relating to the cutting of men's facial
and head hair. Some Christian sects throughout history and up to modern times have also religiously proscribed the
cutting of women's hair. For some Sunni madhabs, the donning of a kufi or topi is a form of sunnah. Brahmin males are
prescribed to shave their heads, but leave a tuft of hair unshaved, worn in the form of a topknot.
In Arabic poetry
Since ancient times, women's long, thick, wavy hair has featured prominently in Arabic poetry. Pre-Islamic poets used
only limited imagery to describe women's hair. For example, al-A'sha wrote a verse comparing a lover's hair to "a
garden whose grapes dangle down upon me", but Bashshar ibn Burd considered this unusual. One comparison used
by early poets, such as Imru al-Qays, was to bunches of dates. In Abbasid times, however, the imagery for hair
expanded significantly - particularly for the then-fashionable "love-locks" (sudgh) framing the temples, which came into
style at the court of the caliph al-Amin. Hair curls were compared to hooks and chains, letters (such as fa, waw, lam,
and nun), scorpions, annelids, and polo sticks. An example was the poet Ibn al-Mu'tazz, who compared a lock of hair
and a birthmark to a polo stick driving a ball.
Hammurabi
Hammurabi (Akkadian: Hammu-rāpi; c. 1810 BC – c. 1750 BC), also spelled Hammurapi, was the sixth Amorite king of
Babylon, reigning from c. 1792 BC to c. 1750 BC. He was preceded by his father, Sin-muballit.
During his reign, he conquered the powerful kingdoms of Larsa, Eshnunna, and Mari, bringing almost all of
<color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color> under Babylonian rule. It was under his rule that Babylon rose to the status of a leading kingdom on the
political stage of the Middle East, and that the foundations were laid for it to become one of the major cities of ancient
history.
Hammurabi is best known for having issued his law code, said to have been inspired by Shamash, the Babylonian god
of Justice. It is one of the oldest legal texts ever discovered, and the longest to have survived from the ancient Near
East. His reign is also one of the Mesopotamian reigns best documented by written records, particularly thanks to the
correspondence unearthed in two of the cities he subjugated, Larsa and Mari, which sheds light on various facets of
how he exercised power during the second half of his reign.
His son Samsu-iluna succeeded him but failed to maintain the empire he had built. After his death, Hammurabi was
revered as a great conqueror, but later his military accomplishments became de-emphasized and his role as the ideal
lawgiver became the primary aspect of his legacy. Hammurabi was rediscovered by archaeologists in the late 19th
century and has since been seen as an important figure in the history of law.
Name
The meaning of the name Hammurabi is a matter of debate. The most common translation is, in Amorite or Akkadian,
“the ancestor is great,” Hammu-rabi, divided in two parts: hammu(m) or ‘ammu, meaning “ancestor,” and rabi, meaning
“great” or “to be great.” An alternative reading, in Amorite, translates the name as “the ancestor heals,” ‘Ammu-rāpi. M.
Streck, for his part, translates ‘ammu as “paternal uncle,” which he interprets as a reference to a protective deity.
This name was borne by kings contemporary with Hammurabi, the most important being Hammurabi I of Yamhad
(Aleppo), as well as by other Amorite kings of Syria who reigned subsequently. It was common among the Amorites for
a man holding the rank of chieftain to bear a name referring to his ancestors, as connection to a lineage and dynastic
continuity were essential to his legitimacy.
Dating
Several factors combine to make reconstructing the chronology of Hammurabi’s reign an approximate endeavor. The
dates given in the rest of this article are established by convention but are clearly inaccurate; the question is to what
extent they are so.
Babylonian sources indicate that Hammurabi reigned for 43 years. The dating system used at the time was based on
year names: each year was named after a significant event that had taken place during the previous year, typically a
religious act (work on a temple, the offering of a divine throne, etc.), a military victory, or the digging of a canal. The
new name for the year was chosen at the end of each year.
Year names of Hammurabi’s reign are all known, which makes it possible to reconstruct the major events of his reign
and place them in chronological order relative to one another.
Ancient texts also make it possible to synchronize Hammurabi’s reign with those of other contemporary rulers
well-documented by sources: his accession occurred while Rim-Sin of Larsa and Samsi-Addu of Ekallatum and Upper
Mesopotamia were in power, and the reign of Zimri-Lim of Mari took place during Hammurabi’s reign. This makes it
possible to establish a relative chronology of his reign, although such synchronizations are often approximate.
Establishing an absolute chronology—that is, assigning dates to Hammurabi's reign within the conventional system of
year-based dating (BC)—is an even more complex matter. Several dating systems have been proposed, "chronologies"
that place Hammurabi's reign at different points in time within a span of nearly two centuries, ranging from the mid-19th
to the mid-17th century BC. The most commonly used system, favored both out of habit and because it is generally
considered the most accurate, is the "Middle" chronology; this places the reign in the middle of that range, from 1792 to
1750 BC (or, according to a proposed revision, from 1784 to 1742 BC). Under the "high" or "long" chronology, which
has few remaining proponents, the reign is placed about half a century earlier, whereas under the "ultra-low"
chronology, the most widely advocated alternative since the late 1990s, Hammurabi's reign would have occurred
approximately a century after the conventionally accepted date.
Reign
Background
Hammurabi’s reign occurred at a pivotal moment in Mesopotamian history. Since the fall of the powerful empire of the
Third Dynasty of Ur (or Ur III) in 2004 BC, Mesopotamia had been divided among several kingdoms ruled by Amorite
dynasties. In the south, the most powerful were first Isin, then Larsa, which attempted to carry on the tradition of the
kings of Ur, but without imposing their hegemony.
Babylon was then merely a secondary city, situated away from the major centers and lacking a notable history, where
an Amorite dynasty took root around 1880 with the accession of Sumu-la-El (1880–1845). He succeeded in carving out
a kingdom that dominated several important neighboring cities (Borsippa, Kish, Kutha, Dilbat, Marad, Sippar). His
successors consolidated the kingdom and thus emerged as increasingly serious rivals to Larsa.
Hammurabi succeeded his father, Sin-muballit, to the throne in 1792 BC. Larsa was in a position of strength during the
early part of the long reign of Rim-Sin (1822-1763 BC), who succeeded in annexing the kingdoms of Isin and Uruk.
Babylon was his most threatening direct rival for hegemony over southern Mesopotamia. In addition to this southern
rival, Babylon had to contend on its northeastern border with the expansionist ambitions of the kingdom of Eshnunna,
whose center was located in the Diyala River Valley. On the other hand, it enjoyed good relations with the strongman of
northern Mesopotamia and rival of Eshnunna, Samsi-Addu (or Shamshi-Adad; 1815-1775 BC), a member of the same
Amorite clan as the kings of Babylon. After spending some time as a refugee in Babylon following a period of unrest, he
settled in the city of Ekallatum, on the Tigris, and within a few years established a powerful kingdom that historians
refer to as the “Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia.” As its name suggests, it dominated the entire northern part of
Mesopotamia, notably incorporating the city of Assur and overshadowing the kings of the Khabur region; then, in 1792
BC, the powerful kingdom of Mari.
Early Years
Hammurabi's date of birth is unknown, as is the age at which he ascended the throne. Given the length of his reign (43
years), he may have been very young at the time, although it is also possible that he was already in his twenties or
even thirties.
The first two decades of his reign are poorly documented. Hammurabi's date of birth is unknown, as is the age at which
he ascended the throne. The names given to the early years of his reign primarily refer to public works and offerings to
deities. His seventh year commemorates a military victory, the capture of Isin and Uruk, territories held by Larsa, but
this was clearly a short-lived raid, as both cities remained under Larsean control. His tenth year commemorates a
victory over Malgium, located east of Babylon, with the support of Samsi-Addu and the king of Eshnunna; but that city
remained independent.
The death of Samsi-Addu in 1775 BC was followed by the rapid disintegration of his kingdom and a struggle for
dominance in Northern Mesopotamia. This competition primarily involved Eshnunna and the new king of Mari,
Zimri-Lim, with whom Hammurabi ultimately formed an alliance.
The War Against Elam
It is from this point on that the letters unearthed at Mari provide a relatively detailed account of international relations,
including those of Babylon. The kingdom of Elam, whose heartland lies in the southwest of present-day <color=#3366CC>Iran</color> (notably at
Susa), and which controlled major trade routes crossing the Iranian Plateau and the Zagros Mountains, decided to
expand into the Mesopotamian plain. It sought to attack the first kingdom in its path, Eshnunna, and easily secured the
support of various kingdoms hostile to Eshnunna, foremost among them Babylon and Mari. Elam attacked and
subjugated the kingdom of Eshnunna. It established its rule over a significant portion of the Mesopotamian plain for the
first time. But Elam did not wish to stop there, which ultimately led to war against Babylon, Mari, and several other
kingdoms in southern and northern Mesopotamia, as well as Syria, which formed a coalition to stop it. The Elamites
then played a double game, in order to sow discord between Rim-Sin of Larsa and Hammurabi of Babylon, just as
these two eternal rivals were trying to reconcile. But the two kings uncovered the ruse, and ultimately formed an
alliance, though the latter contributed little to nothing to the coalition. The Elamites, who were threatening the northern
part of the Babylonian kingdom, were eventually repelled with great difficulty, thanks to the support of troops from Mari
and other kingdoms of northern Mesopotamia.
Major Conquests
Bolstered by this triumph and his alliance with Mari, Hammurabi adopted a more ambitious stance. In the wake of the
withdrawal of the Elamite troops from Eshnunna, he sought to bring that kingdom under his control. A letter from Mari
indicates that he then had the option of either simply annexing the kingdom outright or installing a member of the local
royal family as a puppet ruler (with the approval of the king of Mari). But the elites of Eshnunna made the unexpected
choice to enthrone a section chief—that is, a mere commoner—named Silli-Sin. This led to a year of difficult
negotiations between Babylon and Eshnunna to conclude a peace agreement.
At the same time, Hammurabi launched a lightning war against him with the help of Zimri-Lim of Mari, citing Rim-Sin’s
meager support provided against Elam and his alleged attacks by his troops on his territory, and also taking advantage
of the weakening of his kingdom. He annexed his kingdom in 1763 BC. He thus gained control of the entire lower
Mesopotamian plain. This was a major turning point in the history of the period, as Hammurabi succeeded where many
kings had failed before him for more than two centuries. The fall of the Kingdom of Larsa is recounted in several letters
from Mari soldiers addressed to their king, including this one, written as the final assault was imminent and then carried
out:
Regarding the besieged city of Larsa, I have already written to my lord: “All the refugees who now fall into our hands
say, ‘There is no more grain in the city,’” when in fact there is grain, but without their knowledge. Instead of grain, they
are receiving straw, bran, and chaff… […] After the arrival of reinforcements, the Babylonian troops entered [Larsa] and
seized the walls. This morning, all the men entered. As for Rim-Sin, they brought him out alive.
Continuing his expansion, Hammurabi turned his attention northward. He had resolved to form an alliance with
Eshnunna immediately after his victory over Larsa, and one of his daughters had married its king Silli-Sin. However,
shortly thereafter, he won a victory over Eshnunna, commemorated by the name given to his 32nd regnal year, which
indicates that other neighboring entities (Shubartum and Gutium) were also defeated. The exact circumstances that
triggered this conflict remain unknown, as does the fate of the defeated kingdom.
He then went to war against the region’s other major power, his former ally Zimri-Lim of Mari. The rift between the two
appears to have occurred rapidly, due to Hammurabi’s ambitions in the Jebel Sinjar region, which was under Mari’s
influence. As a result, Zimri-Lim does not appear to have supported him in his conflict against Eshnunna; on the
contrary, he seemed to favor his adversary. The course of the conflict is not documented, but the outcome is clear: Mari
was captured and then destroyed between 1761 BC and 1759 BC. Malgium suffered a similar fate during those same
years.
This led to the end of the Mari archives, and the military history for the remainder of Hammurabi's reign is poorly
documented. The king's year names provide insight into the events deemed most significant by the Babylonian
chancery during the final decade of Hammurabi's reign. Part of the name for the 33rd year (which primarily refers to the
digging of a long canal in the southern part of the kingdom) recounts Hammurabi's new military successes:
The year: Hammu-rabi, the king, […] restored Sumer and Akkad which had been scattered; overthrew in battle the
army of Mari and Malgium; subjugated Mari and its villages and the many cities (of the mountain land) of Subartu,
(Ekallatum, (all of) Burunda and the land of Zalmaqum on the bank of the Tigris up to the Euphrates); and caused to
dwell at his command in friendship.
Hammurabi subsequently consolidated his hold on the north, where he defeated a coalition of kings, including those of
Shubartum, Turukkum, and Gutium (Year Name 37), and then deported people from the conquered lands. In the
process, he established his rule over the city of Assur. The name of Year 39 commemorates another victory in
Shubartum.
According to D. Charpin, the last major potential rival in his neighborhood that had remained independent, Eshnunna,
already greatly weakened, appears to have suffered destruction due to floods (mentioned in the name of the year 38)
and a shift in the course of the Diyala River, which led to its abandonment. During those years, Hammurabi primarily
commemorated several major construction projects, some of which may have been intended to prevent flooding.
Final years
Within a few years, Hammurabi had thus succeeded in uniting Mesopotamia under his rule. One can therefore speak of
an “empire”.
The prologue to the Code of Hammurabi, dated to the end of Hammurabi’s reign, includes a list of major cities under
Babylonian control at that time, which is often used to illustrate the extent of the kingdom after this ruler’s forty-year
reign. Its logic is largely religious, as it first lists city-deity pairs arranged according to a politico-theological objective:
first, the deities who bestowed kingship—Enlil of Nippur, Ea of Eridu, and Marduk of Babylon; then the celestial deities
Sîn of Ur, Shamash of Sippar and Larsa, An and Ishtar of Uruk. The rest follow a more geographical order: cities of
central Babylonia (Isin, Kish, Kutha, Borsippa, Dilbat, Kesh), then cities along the Tigris (Lagash-Girsu, Zabalam,
Karkar, Adab, Mashkan-shapir, Malgium), and finally the major cities of northern Mesopotamia that Hammurabi
conquered toward the end of his reign, namely Mari, Tuttul, Eshnunna, Akkad, Assur, and Nineveh.
Hammurabi died around 1750 BC, in the forty-third year of his reign. His son Samsu-iluna succeeded him. One text
allows us to date the change of reign fairly precisely within the Babylonian calendar, on the tenth day of the fifth month
of the year.
It appears that Hammurabi died of illness, or perhaps of old age, following a period during which he was physically
weakened, beginning in his fortieth year of reign. R. Pientka-Hinz has suggested interpreting the commemorative works
associated with his 40th year, carried out at the sanctuary of Nergal, god of the Underworld, as an indication that he
was already ill at that time and that, sensing his end was near, he wished to curry favor with the lord of the afterlife, who
would soon welcome him.
A letter from his son Samsu-iluna addressed to the governor of Sippar and dated to the final moments of his reign
seems to indicate that Hammurabi was seriously ill at that time and that his death was imminent, but a break in the
tablet prevents the sentence from being fully reconstructed. In any case, his son appears to have been ruling the
kingdom at that time (perhaps as regent) and preparing for his own accession to the throne by remitting debts owed to
servants of the crown, soldiers, and private citizens (muškēnum), measures typically taken upon the ascension of a
new monarch. He also summoned the governor and the Elders, local political authorities, from his province to the
capital.
Family
Hammurabi's family is very poorly known.
None of his wives are documented, but based on the customs of his time, he must have had at least one (or even two)
principal wife(s), secondary wives, and numerous concubines, with a harem, which was enlarged, notably following his
military conquests.
One of Hammurabi's sisters is known: Iltani, who became a nun (nadītum) devoted to the god Shamash at Sippar, a
common practice among royal families of the time, serving to strengthen the bonds between kings and the gods. None
of his brothers are known, but a text from Larsa seems to mention an unnamed "daughter of the king's brother,"
therefore a niece of a brother, perhaps who became a priestess of the god Shamash in that city. From known examples
in other kingdoms of his time, the sovereign's brothers were often involved at the highest level in the affairs of the
kingdom.
Two of his sons are attested in the archives of Mari: Sumu-ditana (the eldest son?) and Mutu-Numaha, whose names
referred to ancestors of his dynasty. They were both sent to Mari for a time as part of educational journeys, which
appear to have been a custom at the time. They may also have served as hostages when the king of Mari was lending
troops to Babylon. The son destined to succeed Hammurabi, Samsu-iluna, is not attested during his reign. It is not
known whether he is the eldest of the siblings, as he was to proclaim in one of his own royal inscriptions.
Among his daughters, at least one in turn becomes a nun devoted to Shamash, perhaps called Lamassani, and
another is married to the king Silli-Sin of Eshnunna.
Government
Ideology of Kingship
Toward the end of his reign, the prologue to the Code of Hammurabi extols the greatness of the ruler, who had reached
the height of his glory following his great conquests. It notably encompasses the two aspects of Mesopotamian royal
legitimacy: divine election, particularly through references to the deities who bestow sovereignty (Enlil, Marduk, Ishtar);
and descent from a royal dynasty, through reference to the founder of Hammurabi’s dynasty, Sumu-la-El (1880–1845),
and to his father and immediate predecessor, Sin-muballit (1812–1793 BC)..
I am Hammurabi, the shepherd, selected by the god Enlil, he who heaps abundance and plenty, who perfects every
possible thing for the city Nippur, (the city known as) bond-of-heaven-and-earth, the pious provider of the Ekur temple;
[...] the onslaught of the four regions of the world, who magnifies the reputation of the city Babylon, who gladdens the
heart of his divine lord Marduk, whose days are devoted to the Esagil temple; [...]
the pious one, who prays ceaselessly for the great gods, scion of Sumu-la-El, mighty heir of Sin-muballit, eternal seed
of royalty, mighty king, solar disk of the city of Babylon, who spreads light over the lands of Sumer and Akkad, king who
makes the four regions obedient, favored of the goddess Ishtar, am I.
The official inscriptions celebrating Hammurabi emphasize his personal qualities—that he was a “strong king,” an
“accomplished king,” and a “hero.” Hammurabi’s titles refer more simply to his status, which grew increasingly imposing
as his conquests progressed: he was initially defined simply as “king of Babylon,” and after the conquest of Larsa and
his assumption of control over all of southern Mesopotamia, he adopted the prestigious title of “king of the lands of
<color=#3366CC>Sumer</color> and Akkad,” which had been borne by the kings of the Third Dynasty of Ur. After the conquest of Mari, he added
“king of the entire Amorite land” to his titles, and by the end of his reign he was “king of the four regions/quarters” of the
world—that is, he claimed universal dominion.
Hammurabi even attained a form of divinization following the conquest of the Kingdom of Larsa and the incorporation of
the ancient land of <color=#3366CC>Sumer</color>, where the tradition of divine kingship was more deeply rooted than in the region of Babylon.
The king's name is sometimes written in cuneiform preceded by the sign indicating divine nature, and an inscription
defines him as the "god of his land," while also noting his obedience and devotion to the great gods.
Several hymns in Sumerian, or in both Sumerian and Akkadian, focus on Hammurabi, singing the king's praises. They
often take the form of hymns addressed to a deity (Enki, Asarluhi, Inanna) that conclude with a prayer for the king's
well-being.
The subjects of the kingdom were expected to offer prayers and gifts to the gods and goddess so as to secure their
protection and favor for the king, or, according to the established formula, “for his life.” This was, therefore, a way of
demonstrating allegiance to the king. Votive objects were also offered to the gods by the subjects of Babylon on behalf
of their king: the Worshipper of Larsa, a statue bearing an inscription requesting the intercession of the god Amurrum
on behalf of Hammurabi, as well as in a fragment of a sculpture likely from Sippar, which invokes the goddess
Ashratum (Amurrum’s wife).
Hammurabi's Court
In principle, the king resides in a "palace" (ekallum), a term denoting not only the building itself but also the royal
institution and its estates. While Hammurabi certainly had a palace in Babylon (which was not uncovered during
excavations of the city), he also resided in other cities within his kingdom where he maintained provincial palaces,
notably in the vicinity of Babylon (Sippar, Borsippa, Kish), and, following the conquest of Larsa, in the former royal
palaces of the Amorite dynasties of <color=#3366CC>Sumer</color> (Larsa, Uruk, Isin). A palace of Hammurabi has been identified by an
inscription at the site of Tell Muhammad (near Baghdad), within the territories seized from Eshnunna.
Hammurabi governed while surrounded by figures akin to "ministers." While each held a specific portfolio, they could
also, depending on the king's will, carry out distinct, ad hoc assignments as needed. The Mari letters reveal two of
Hammurabi's key ministers who held the title of šukkallum (often translated as "vizier"): Erra-nada and Sin-bel-aplim,
the latter being specifically responsible for receiving foreign embassies. He also had private secretaries, responsible for
his correspondence, who were privy to the highest levels of state secrets; letters from Mari identify Sin-iddinam (who
later became governor of Larsa; see below) and Marduk-nasir as holders of this position. Other high-ranking figures
with less clearly defined roles are attested in texts as belonging to Hammurabi's inner circle.
Seals also provide a valuable source for understanding the Babylonian administration: a cylinder seal and several
cylinder seal impressions found on tablets bear inscriptions identifying individuals who describe themselves as "servant
of Hammurabi," a designation generally interpreted as indicating that they were palace officials.
In any case, it appears that personal ties to the king were the primary factor in the selection of the ruling elite. The king
made decisions with the support of a council, literally the "secret" (pirištum). He admitted whomever he chose to this
body and could therefore alter its composition at will. A letter from Mari reveals that, during the war against Elam,
Hammurabi brought three high-ranking officials who had served Ishme-Dagan of Ekallatum (son of Samsi-Addu) into
his council; these men sidelined officials originally from Babylon and held the privilege of learning the results of oracular
consultations.
Major Public Works
Another essential characteristic of the Mesopotamian royal office that Hammurabi undertook was large-scale public
works projects, which involved both the countryside and the cities.
The digging of canals for irrigation and transportation frequently appears in the regnal years of the kings of the Amorite
period, and Hammurabi was no exception. Thus, the 33rd year of his reign commemorates the completion of a canal
named in his honor, “Hammurabi (brings) abundance to the people” (in Akkadian Hammu-rabi nuhuš nishī):
This construction should be viewed in the context of the various projects undertaken in the territories of the former
kingdom of Larsa following its conquest. As the canal’s name suggests, in royal ideology this reflects the ability of a
good ruler to ensure the prosperity of his people. Two other year names, several commemorative inscriptions, and the
prologue to the Code of Hammurabi mention similar undertakings.
Mesopotamian rulers also frequently undertook the construction or repair of city walls, thereby ensuring the protection
of the people. Several of Hammurabi’s inscriptions refer to the reconstruction of the city walls of Sippar, which is also
the subject of the name of the year Hammurabi 23. Once again, the structure bears a name in honor of the king, "By
the decree of the god Shamash, may Hammurabi have no rival," invoking the protection granted to him by the local
god.
Larsa after its conquest
Hammurabi's administrative actions are primarily documented by a corpus of over 200 letters found at Larsa that he
addressed to subordinates stationed in the city. Their exact provenance is unknown, as they come from illicit
excavations carried out in the early 20th century.
Following the conquest of the kingdom in 1764/63 BC, its royal domain was incorporated into Hammurabi's, and its
resources were subsequently redirected to Babylon at the sovereign's behest.. However, there appear to have been no
significant land confiscations at that time; landholders generally remained the same as before. The province of the city
of Larsa was entrusted to a certain Sin-iddinam, who oversaw the transition from Larsa's control to Babylonian rule,
specifically by enforcing Babylonian law in place of the traditional law of the region. The approximately one hundred
letters addressed to him by Hammurabi cover a variety of subjects: the management of the irrigation system and
military troops, tax collection, the organization of corvée labor and the workforce, the shipment of goods and animals to
Babylon, various legal matters, and even police activities. For instance, in the following letter, Hammurabi asks him to
handle a case of corruption:
The other primary recipient of the letters from Hammurabi discovered at Larsa was Shamash-hazir, the "head of the
land registry" and administrator of palace estates in the Larsa region. The letters addressed to him deal primarily with
the allocation of service lands (ilkum), which were granted to individuals in exchange for services rendered to the crown
(military, crafts, etc.). These allocations frequently gave rise to disputes, as the lands were often appropriated by
unauthorized parties, necessitating field investigations conducted by Shamash-hazir himself.
Correspondence sent by Hammurabi to his administrators reveals that the king often involved himself personally and
directly in provincial affairs. He was frequently petitioned by his subjects regarding legal disputes and issues
concerning land allocation, and he would order his subordinates to investigate and report back to him in detail. It
mattered little to him whether the matter was significant or not.
The annexation of Larsa also appears to have had a significant cultural impact on the Kingdom of Babylon, resulting
from the integration of members of the former kingdom's educated elite, particularly those versed in Sumerian texts.
This is notably evident in royal inscriptions, which were composed in Sumerian following the conquest of Larsa,
whereas they had previously been in Akkadian. This influx appears to have profoundly influenced the political and
religious ideology, literature, religious practice, and statecraft of the Babylonian kingdom, which had previously held a
somewhat secondary cultural position.
Divine Cults
As the chosen one of the gods, Hammurabi must also ensure that the worship of the gods proceeds smoothly; in turn,
they guaranteed the prosperity of his kingdom. Consequently, the construction or restoration of sanctuaries features
prominently in commemorative texts. For instance, the reconstruction of the ziggurat (a stepped tower) at the sanctuary
of the warrior god Zababa in Kish (where the goddess Inanna/Ishtar was also venerated) is commemorated by several
inscriptions in two variants (the longer of which is translated here) and by a year name (Hammurabi 36).
Furthermore, several of his year names commemorate votive offerings, such as the fourteenth year: "Year in which
Hammu rabi the king made for Inanna of Babylon a magnificent throne dais, adorned with gold, silver, eye-hulalu-stone,
muszszaru-stone and lapis-lazuli flashing like rays and made her chariot complete in everything."
A few letters from Larsa also document concerns regarding cultic matters: the organization of the transport of statues of
goddesses, and the collection of silver for a temple.
A sister and a daughter of Hammurabi were also nadītum priestesses dedicated to another major deity, Shamash of
Sippar, yet another manifestation of the ties between the king and the gods, which is part of an older tradition of strong
ties between the Babylonian dynasty and the great sanctuary of Sippar.
The king consulted the gods through divination. This could involve the appointment of an official, the advisability of an
alliance, or, quite frequently, military matters, and more generally, anything concerning the kingdom and the king. The
most common form of divination practiced at the royal courts of this period was hepatoscopy, divination using the liver
of a lamb, a practice best attested in the archives of Mari. A tablet dating to the 1st millennium BC records several
oracular consultations from the reign of Hammurabi regarding military campaigns, notably the capture of the city of
Kazallu. Despite the late date of the tablet itself, its authenticity appears to be established. An instance of prophecy at
the Babylonian court is also attested in a letter from Mari: a prophet of the god Marduk appeared at the palace gate to
berate Ishme-Dagan of Ekallatum, who was present there, accusing him of preferring to hand over his possessions to
the king of Elam rather than consecrating them to the god.
Justice and Law
The King of Justice
The ideal Mesopotamian king's role is to administer justice and protect the weak against the powerful. In the case of
Hammurabi, this is eloquently illustrated in his famous Code of Hammurabi. The top of the stele depicts the king facing
the sun god Shamash, the deity of justice, who inspires the judgments he passes and which are recorded on the stele.
The monarch is presented in the stele's epilogue as a recourse against injustices, including those arising from the
routine administration of justice. Several laws of the Code of Hammurabi deal with the probity of judges, which again
refers to the role of the king as guarantor of justice and protector of those subject to the law. The king is also invoked in
the oaths taken during trials, alongside deities.
In practice, the king could intervene directly in the judicial life of his kingdom. The letters from Larsa thus indicate that
he was involved in matters concerning the royal domain, and more generally its administration. Governor Sin-iddinam
was often called upon to find witnesses and evidence so that the king could make a decision. Hammurabi intervened at
the request of those involved in the case, and the matter could then be decided in different ways: either the king himself
rendered the verdict; either the king issues a ruling on a point of law, which the local judges then enforce; or he refers
the case back to the local judges, requesting to be kept informed of its progress. Letters from Larsa indicate that the
king is not necessarily the one who passes judgments in Babylon, since in several cases this task falls to a certain
Awil-Ninurta, perhaps a "minister".
The king also has a role in social justice, that is, a responsibility to ensure fairness. He is expected to put an end to
situations of glaring inequality—particularly during economic crises—by issuing edicts of debt remission known as
andurarum and mišarum (which appear to have primarily targeted loans for necessities, not commercial loans).
Hammurabi issued one during his first year of reign (1792/1791 BCE) and commemorated this in the name of his
second year of reign, “Year in which King Hammurabi established law and justice in his land.” He then promulgated
another one in the land of Larsa after its conquest (1763 BC). This goal of "economic justice" is also reflected in various
articles of the Code of Hammurabi, which specify prices for various types of services; these appear to correspond to
the idea of a “fair price”—a threshold below which the situation was considered unjust for the person being paid.
The Code of Hammurabi
The Code of Hammurabi derives directly from this function of the king as guardian of justice and equity. It is divided into
three parts: a prologue, a set of law provisions, and an epilogue. Written towards the end of Hammurabi's reign and
known primarily from a large stela on which it was inscribed (tablets also document parts of the text), its status is
debated. This is certainly not the only known Mesopotamian legislative collection, nor the oldest, but it is the longest
known. In many respects, especially as expressed in the prologue and epilogue, it presents itself as a commemorative
inscription celebrating Hammurabi's sense of justice and intended to preserve his memory for posterity.
These are the just decisions which Hammurabi, the able king, has established and therevy has directed the land along
the course of truth and the correct way of life. [...] In order that the mighty not wrong the weak, to provide just ways for
the waif and the widow, I have inscribed my precious prononcements upon my stela and set it up before the statue of
me, the king of justice, in the city of Babylon [...] Let any wronged man whi has a lawsuit come before the statue of me,
the king of justice, and let him have my inscribed stela read aloud to him, thus may he hear my precious
prononcements and let my stela reveal the lawsuit for him; may he examine his case, may he calm his (troubled) heart
The "laws" are thus a manifestation of the qualities of the just king. Divided by modern historians into 282 "law
provisions" (or rules), they are arranged thematically, addressing various subjects: judicial practices, infringements on
property rights, agrarian structures, financial matters, family law, assault and battery, provisions concerning various
professions, and the ownership of slaves.
The nature and function of these laws are debated. Many see them as a scholarly and technical exercise, carried out
by scribes, certainly based on the legal practices of the time, and therefore more a description of the law and a
reflection on just decisions than prescriptions on the norms to be applied. It is possible that a number of these laws
were written based on cases actually judged by Hammurabi. Some specialists believe that they may have served, at
the very least, as examples, as models, for those who had to administer justice. However, without conclusive proof of
their application in the judgments known from other cuneiform texts of the same period, they do not go further. But
others do, analyzing them as a kind of rescript, general solutions derived from particular cases, which could (should?)
indeed be applied by judges.
Hammurabi's legislative action may have aimed to modify and unify the various customs existing in the territories he
brought under his control, at least in certain areas of greatest concern to the monarch, since the Laws does not cover
all aspects of legal life, far from it. Moreover, these objectives remain largely theoretical. In general, the purpose of the
laws seems to be at least to define the practices of a written law, with sealed tablets authenticable by witnesses; to
establish obligations of social responsibility on the part of the kingdom's subjects; and to define the role of local
institutions in relation to individuals by more strictly regulating their actions, particularly in the administration of justice,
perhaps to weaken them.
War and Diplomacy
The King of War
War held an important place in the ideology of Mesopotamian kingship. According to the prevailing ideology of the time,
the support of the gods was necessary for victory, and Hammurabi sought their advice through divination before
undertaking a battle. A hymn for the king, formulated as an oracular text, urged him to take action and extend his
kingdom and renown throughout the world, for he had received the approval of the major gods and goddesses.
But was Hammurabi a warlike king? His reign was marked by numerous conflicts, but his inscriptions do not portray him
as a warmonger; on the contrary, he comes across as someone who is forced to take part in military conflicts, against
his will. In any case, Hammurabi seems to have achieved his conquests primarily by seizing opportunities that
presented themselves, without a pre-conceived imperialist project.
During wars, the king kept himself informed of the progress of operations, commanded the movements of the troops,
and communicated with his allies. Some of the rare letters from Hammurabi found in Mariinform his ally Zimri-Lim and
his subordinates of the latest news of the campaign against the Elamite army, so as to coordinate the actions of the
coalition troops. It also seems that it was expected that the king would review his troops before battle, war being one of
the main occasions during which a ruler was in contact with his people. A letter from Mari reports the speech delivered
by Hammurabi to his soldiers before the assault on Mashkan-shapir, in which he proclaims that he is in the right when
facing his enemy, Rim-Sin of Larsa, which has been confirmed by oracular consultations with Marduk and Shamash,
and at the same time asks for clemency if the city capitulates:
In the light of the numerous conflicts that marked Hammurabi's reign, it is hardly surprising that concerns about military
resources (recruitment, financing of equipment, aid from allied kingdoms) appear repeatedly in the documentation. A
large section of the Code of Hammurabi (§ 26-41) is devoted to the status of soldiers. They are divided into two
categories: the rēdum, literally 'the one who follows', a kind of infantryman, and the bā'irum, literally 'fisherman', a
soldier who patrols on boats (on waterways). Desertion is punishable by death. The Larsa tablets reflect the same
concerns: military records indicate that after the annexation of the territory, Hammurabi ordered a census, seemingly
intended to determine who could be mobilized for his army. Governor Sin-iddinam was regularly called upon to raise
troops. Shamash-hazir, for his part, was responsible for allocating land from the royal domain to soldiers.
Diplomatic Communications
Hammurabi was among the most powerful kings of his time, who dominated the international stage, alongside the kings
of Mari, Yamhad (Aleppo), Qatna, Larsa, Eshnunna, and Elam (the latter apparently ranking even higher than the
others, at least before his defeat). In the diplomatic vocabulary of the time, they regarded themselves as “brothers”, i.e.
equals. In contrast, kings of secondary rank were their “sons,” and they were expected to regard them as their “fathers.”
Normal relations between royal courts involved the exchange of messengers representing a king, who would send
them to the court of another ruler (there were no permanent embassies). They might be tasked with delivering the gifts
that kings exchanged with one another, or even negotiations between the two courts. The letters report various royal
audiences, sometimes marred by incidents, as in this case where the Mariotes sent at the Babylonian court complain of
not being treated with the same deference as the representatives of the kingdom of Yamhad:
We entered to take a meal in Hammurabi’s presence, moving into the Palace Court. Just the three of us—Zimri-Addu, I,
and Yarim-Addu—were provided with garments, whereas the Yamhad (delegates) that entered with us were all
outfitted. As all the Yamhadians were outfitted but they did not outfit the attachés (ša sikkim), my lord’s servants, I told
Sin-bel-aplim (Hammurabi’s chief-of-staff) on their behalf, “Why do you segregate us as if the brood of a sow? Whose
servants are we, and whose servants are these attachés? We are all the servants [of the same king], so why would you
pit the right against the left?” This is what I stressed to Sin-bel-aplim. While I was arguing with Sin-bel-aplim, my lord’s
servants, the attachés, got angry and stormed out of the Palace Court. Hammurabi was told of the matter, and
subsequently they were outfitted. Once they were outfitted, Tab-eli-matim and Sin-bel-aplim (summoned me) and told
me (what) Hammurabi had said, “Since early morning, you keep obstructing me with provocative words. Do you now
dictate to my palace about garment (distribution)? Whoever pleases me, I outfit; whoever does not, I don’t. I won’t come
back (on this): I will not outfit messengers at banquets!” This is what Hammurabi told me; my lord should know this.
We know from other examples that Hammurabi treated foreign messengers according to the nature of his relations with
their ruler: Elamite messengers were thus given small portions of food when the two countries were at war, but were
treated more favorably once the Elamite troops had left Mesopotamia.
Alliances
Diplomatic agreements were commonplace in the Amorite Middle East, and the period of coalition formation against
Elam saw several agreements negotiated and concluded by Hammurabi. The essential element of the alliance ritual
was the taking of an oath, for which the two kings did not need to meet in person. Instead of a peace treaty, a protocol
of oath containing the clauses of the agreement was drawn up and recited before divine symbols, accompanied by
ritual gestures. A letter from Mari recounts the proceedings of the alliance between Hammurabi and Silli-Sin of
Eshnunna. The negotiations concerning the diplomatic agreement between Hammurabi and Zimri-Lim against Elam are
documented by several tablets. For a time, the dispute between the two kingdoms over the control of the city of Hit
posed an obstacle, but it was set aside so as not to hinder the alliance. Then came issues related to the ritual gestures
and timing of the oath-taking. One letter indicates that Hammurabi was alarmed by the severity of the curses included
in the agreement, divine punishments meant to befall anyone who broke the contract. Another shows that the
Babylonian king refused to commit on the 25th of the month, apparently a day considered unlucky for invoking the
name of the moon god Sin, and instead took the oath three days later before his council. The oath protocol sworn by
Hammurabi was preserved by his partner, Zimri-Lim, and found in the archives of Mari. Similarly, Hammurabi must
have kept the oath protocol of Zimri-Lim in his own archives:
Interdynastic marriages are another important aspect of diplomatic alliances. Regarding Hammurabi, only the marriage
between one of his daughters and the king Silli-Sin of Eshnunna is known, which must take place when the alliance
between the two was concluded.
Personality and Political Skills
Letters from Mari, which are the only documents that depict Hammurabi through his daily actions and words, reveal him
to be a skilled negotiator, reluctant to yield to the wishes of his allies, even when he needed their support. While he
clearly commanded an effective army, he was also a shrewd diplomat. This is particularly evident in the negotiations
surrounding the city of Hit, which was disputed between Babylon and Mari; these negotiations temporarily hindered an
alliance between the two, despite the Elamite invasion, which directly threatened Babylon and in the face of which
Babylon needed Mari’s support. The issue was left unresolved in order to allow the alliance to proceed. But this did not
prevent Hammurabi from rejecting Mari’s demands and reiterating his claims to the city and their justification, namely,
the fact that the city possessed the naphtha necessary for caulking ships, a crucial means of transportation in southern
Mesopotamia due to its numerous waterways. This further highlights the Babylonian king's keen awareness of the
importance of securing access to raw materials necessary for his country.
Hammurabi thus knows how to use his allies to his advantage, while giving them as little as possible, a fact that Mari
learned the hard way. He also ensures that his status is respected and does not allow kings of lower rank to take
advantage of him. For example, a letter recounts a tense audience between Hammurabi and emissaries from
Ishme-Dagan of Ekallatum, a longtime ally and distant relative of Hammurabi. The exchange concerns various
complaints by Ishme-Dagan, first regarding the fact that he had not received troops from Hammurabi—unlike other
kings in northern Mesopotamia—despite the aid he had provided to Hammurabi in the past. This is followed by
recriminations regarding Mari, which the messengers from Ekallatum apparently sought to gloss over. All of this
provoked several outbursts of anger from Hammurabi:
Hammurabi answered them thus: “To whom have I given troops? Tell me, tell me!” Approaching them, he repeated his
question five or six times, obliging them to answer: “You gave troops to Atamrum (a king of northern Mesopotamia)!”
And Hammurabi answered them: “What troops did I give to Atamrum? It was a troop of 300 or 400 men (only) that I
sent to Atamrum, and the troop […] (Gap). Hammurabi replied: “Why are you withholding the rest of your report? Tell
me your full report.” They said: “[…]”… He said: “Surely there is other news you carry.” They said, “No, [we have not
concealed] a secret report that your servant (Ishme-Dagan) sent you. Do not force us: our lord is spread out beneath
your feet like a rug. Even if there is another king who reveres you, he does not write such messages of submission to
you.” When Ishme-Dagan’s messengers said this, Hammurabi replied to them, “Since you do not wish to complete your
report, let my servant who came with you complete it!” Hammurabi summoned his servant who had come with them
and said to him, “Since they do not wish to complete the report they were charged with, it is your turn! You, complete
their report!” Hammurabi’s servant who had come with them [came]; after repeating the report delivered by the
messengers of Ishme-Dagan, he added to it, saying: “Zimri-Lim, to whom you have me writing as a son, is he not my
servant? He does not dwell on a high throne; therefore, I have not written exalted greetings.” When he heard these
words, Hammurabi cried out, “What a scandal!” The messengers of Ishme-Dagan denied this report. […]
We thus gain a rare glimpse into Hammurabi’s personality, which is portrayed here as hot-tempered, impatient, and
threatening toward the envoys from Ekallatum, a “volatile” personality, according to K. Radner.
Beyond the image of a just king that he wished to project, Hammurabi caused widespread devastation during his
conquests. For this reason, P. Michalowski points out that he can be viewed as a “tyrant.” On several occasions,
Hammurabi ordered acts of destruction, such as the destruction of the palace at Mari, as well as the deportation of the
defeated, as after the Mutiabal revolt. On the other hand, however, these were not unusual acts for his own time, and
there is no indication that he was any more brutal than other kings of his era.
The letters addressed to his subordinates in Larsa portray him as a king deeply involved in the affairs of his realm and
close to his subjects, according to M. Van De Mieroop: "Hammurabi’s management style was very direct and the letters
indicate that anyone could turn to him when facing a problem. He either rendered a verdict and directed his officials to
carry out his orders, or he asked them to investigate the matter further. Nothing seems to have been too trivial for his
attention. He asked about small lots of land, single servants, and so on. Some scholars have seen this as a sign that he
was a petty ruler, but that is a mistaken judgment. Hammurabi properly fulfilled his functions as king. He was there for
his people and all were allowed to approach him. This created a personal bond between the king and his people."
According to P.-A. Beaulieu, this level of involvement may indicate that he sought to combat corruption and the
formation of fiefdoms that would threaten the integrity of his state, which would then explain his success as a
kingdom-builder.
Did Hammurabi intend to build an empire modeled on those of the Akkadian and Ur III dynasties? It is impossible to say
for certain, but judging by the course of the conquests, the existence of a carefully crafted plan from the very beginning
of his reign seems unlikely. According to D. Charpin, "it is likely that the empire was the result not so much of a
deliberate policy as of the skillful exploitation of successive opportunities." The sequence of conquests gives the
impression of a single, unplanned military campaign. The kingdom's expansion took place over just a few years,
beginning with a defensive response to the Elamite invasion and continuing through a series of conflicts against major
rival powers—all apparently without demobilizing his army.
At the very least, this credits Hammurabi with great political acumen and the ability to make the most of opportunities
presented by the highly fluid international landscape of the time. According to P.-A. Beaulieu: "It is tempting for
historians to explain retrospectively the success of Babylon by highlighting economic, geographic, or environmental
conditions that would have made its rise inevitable. Such factors always play a role in history, but none should be
considered decisive and Hammu-rabi must also receive some individual credit. A less capable and astute leader might
easily have failed, letting other cities make their bid to unify Mesopotamia under a single administration."
Legacy
Aftermath
Hammurabi's conquests were considerable: in just a few years, he eliminated the major kingdoms of Larsa, Mari, and
Eshnunna. Babylon, at the beginning of his reign, was a kingdom with limited territory, facing numerous rivals. By his
death, it was the dominant power in <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>, and the two other major powers of the Middle East, Yamhad
(Aleppo) and Elam, being further away, were no longer a threat. Hammurabi's victories had the lasting consequence of
disrupting the balance of power that had existed since the fall of the Third Dynasty of Ur, and which had allowed the
Amorite dynasties to flourish.
After Hammurabi's death, his son and successor Samsu-iluna (1749-1712 BC) failed to preserve the empire he
inherited: several revolts led to the loss of the southern part of the kingdom (the former territories of Larsa), which
became depopulated, while his attempts to extend and strengthen Babylonian rule in the north did not achieve lasting
success. Nevertheless, Hammurabi's dynasty survived for several more decades. The 17th century BC saw the
following Babylonian kings maintain their control over the heart of the kingdom, however precariously. But their power
declined inexorably in the face of the emergence of the First Sealand dynasty in the south, and Kassite dynasties in the
north. Hammurabi's dynasty was brought to an end by a Hittite attack in 1595 BC.
Hammurabi's conquests and empire were therefore short-lived. The revolts faced by Samsu-iluna, followed by the rise
of the Sealand, indicate that the defeated cities and regions had not fully accepted the loss of their independence. The
unification of Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule was thus a brief phenomenon: it began in the second half of his
reign, and his successor lost it. The conquered regions north of Babylonia were never held permanently. It can
nevertheless be considered that Hammurabi laid the foundations for a unification of Lower Mesopotamia, relegating the
capitals of the ancient kingdoms to the status of provincial towns, and that his reign was an important part of a broader
long-term dynamic which saw the affirmation of territorial states in the Middle East.
Ancient commemorations
Hammurabi was honored above all other kings of the second millennium BC and he received the unique honor of being
declared to be a god within his own lifetime. The personal name "Hammurabi-ili" meaning "Hammurabi is my god"
became common during and after his reign. In writings from shortly after his death, Hammurabi is commemorated
mainly for three achievements: bringing victory in war, bringing peace, and bringing justice. Hammurabi's conquests
came to be regarded as part of a sacred mission to spread civilization to all nations. A stele from Ur glorifies him in his
own voice as a mighty ruler who forces evil into submission and compels all peoples to worship Marduk. The stele
declares: "The people of Elam, Gutium, Subartu, and Tukrish, whose mountains are distant and whose languages are
obscure, I placed into [Marduk's] hand. I myself continued to put straight their confused minds." A later hymn also
written in Hammurabi's own voice extols him as a powerful, supernatural force for Marduk:
I am the king, the brace that grasps wrongdoers, that makes people of one mind, I am the great dragon among kings,
who throws their counsel in disarray, I am the net that is stretched over the enemy, I am the fear-inspiring, who, when
lifting his fierce eyes, gives the disobedient the death sentence, I am the great net that covers evil intent, I am the
young lion, who breaks nets and scepters, I am the battle net that catches him who offends me.
After extolling Hammurabi's military accomplishments, the hymn finally declares: "I am Hammurabi, the king of justice."
In later commemorations, Hammurabi's role as a great lawgiver came to be emphasized above all his other
accomplishments and his military achievements became de-emphasized. Hammurabi's reign became the point of
reference for all events in the distant past. A hymn to the goddess Ishtar, whose language suggests it was written
during the reign of Ammi-Saduqa, Hammurabi's fourth successor, declares: "The king who first heard this song as a
song of your heroism is Hammurabi. This song for you was composed in his reign. May he be given life forever!" For
centuries after his death, Hammurabi's laws continued to be copied by scribes as part of their writing exercises and
they were even partially translated into Sumerian.
Over a thousand years after Hammurabi's death, the kings of Suhum, a land along the Euphrates River, just northwest
of Babylon, claimed him as their ancestor.
A Neo-Babylonian royal inscription, which was intended for display on a stele, commemorates a royal grant of tax
exemptions to nine Babylonian cities and presents the royal protagonist as a second Hammurabi.
Modern receptions
The name of Hammurabi re-emerges from the mists of history in the mid-19th century, when excavations of ancient
Mesopotamian sites began and cuneiform writing was deciphered. Two bronze pommels excavated in 1850 at Tell
Muhammad bear an inscription referring to the "Palace of Hammurabi," which was not properly deciphered until later.
Following the rediscovery of other inscriptions bearing the name of this king, the French assyriologist Joachim Menant
published in 1863 the first collection of texts entirely devoted to the king. The stature of this king reached a major level
in 1901–1902, when the stela of his Code of Hammurabi was unearthed at Susa. Discovered by a French
archaeological team, its long inscription was translated and immediately published by Jean-Vincent Scheil.
In the early twentieth century, many scholars believed that Hammurabi was Amraphel, the King of Shinar in the Book of
Genesis 14:1. This view has now been largely rejected, and Amraphel's existence is not attested in any writings from
outside the Bible.
Because of Hammurabi's reputation as a lawgiver, his depiction can be found in law buildings throughout the world.
Hammurabi is one of the 23 lawgivers depicted in marble bas-reliefs in the chamber of the U.S. House of
Representatives in the United States Capitol. A frieze by Adolph Weinman depicting the "great lawgivers of history",
including Hammurabi, is on the south wall of the U.S. Supreme Court building.
Hammurabi's legacy was also claimed by Saddam Hussein, who sought to reappropriate the great figures of ancient
Mesopotamia to consolidate his power. He had a bronze statue of the king, measuring over 4 meters, placed at the
entrance to the Iraqi Parliament, in reference to his role as a legislator.
Han dynasty
The Han dynasty (202 BC – 9 AD, 25–220 AD) was an imperial dynasty of China established by Liu Bang, and
preceded by the short-lived Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) and the interregnum known as the Chu–Han Contention
(206–202 BC). It was succeeded by the Three Kingdoms period (220–280 AD) and also briefly interrupted by the Xin
dynasty (9–23 AD) established by the usurping regent Wang Mang. It is thus separated into two periods—the Western
Han (202 BC – 9 AD) and the Eastern Han (25–220 AD). The Han dynasty is considered a golden age in Chinese
history, impacting Chinese identity in later periods. The majority ethnic group of modern <color=#3366CC>China</color> refer to themselves as
the "Han people", while spoken Chinese and written Chinese are referred to respectively as the "<color=#3366CC>Han language</color>" and
"Han characters".
The Han emperor was at the pinnacle of Han society and culture. He presided over the Han government but shared
power with both the nobility and the appointed ministers, who came largely from the scholarly gentry class. The Han
Empire was divided into commanderies directly controlled by the central government and also semi-autonomous
kingdoms. These kingdoms gradually lost their autonomy, particularly following the Rebellion of the Seven States. From
the reign of Emperor Wu (r. 141–87 BC) onward, the Chinese court officially sponsored <color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color> in education and
court politics, synthesizing it with the cosmology of Dong Zhongshu. The Han dynasty experienced periods of economic
prosperity as well as significant growth in the money economy, which had first been established during the Zhou
